summary: Defines the requirements for dynamic directory services in LDAPv3 and the format of request and response extended operations to support them. It lets directory entries expire unless refreshed.

plainLanguage.summary: Some directory entries should disappear on their own if nobody keeps them fresh, like a sign that falls down unless you keep re-posting it.

questions: what is an ldap dynamic entry
what is the dynamicobject object class
subtitle: Directory entries that vanish on their own unless the client keeps refreshing them.

tldr.problem: LDAP was built for static directory data, but some information, such as whether a person or client is online, is only accurate while someone keeps vouching for it.
tldr.mechanism: A dynamic entry carries a time-to-live. The client sends a Refresh extended operation at intervals to reset it, and the server removes the entry on its own if refreshes stop.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers get a standard, LDAP-integrated way to publish short-lived entries. Servers can shorten requested lifetimes, but not below one day.

facts.label: Shortest TTL a server may impose

today: RFC 2589 is a Proposed Standard from May 1999. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Static and Dynamic Directories
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) gives fast search and update access to static directory data, which stays accurate and valuable over a long time. Dynamic directory data is different: it only stays accurate while it is being periodically refreshed.

A typical case is a client or person who is online and so has an entry, or is offline and so has none. If a dynamic entry is not refreshed within its timeout, the server removes it. The memo also describes a flow control mechanism that lets the server tell clients how often to refresh.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal directory is like a printed phone book. A dynamic one is like a whiteboard that says who is here right now, and names get wiped off if people stop checking in.

sections.title: What the Extension Must Do
sections.content:
The extensions must let clients reach dynamic information in the standard LDAP manner, so static and dynamic data are accessed the same way. The server needs a scalable way to tell whether entries are still valid, and clients need a way to re-establish an entry.

Clients must also be able to discover, in a standard LDAP manner, whether a server supports the extensions. Finally, the extensions need to be registered as standard LDAP extended operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say the new whiteboard must work like the old phone book, let people re-write their name if it got wiped, and let you ask whether a given office even has a whiteboard.

sections.title: Dynamic Entries and Meetings
sections.content:
A dynamic entry is a directory object with a time-to-live set when it is created. The time-to-live counts down, and when it expires the entry disappears. A client resets it with the refresh extended operation. An entry becomes dynamic when the dynamicObject object class is included at creation, subject to the usual access control.

Dynamic entries are treated like static ones for search, compare, add, delete, modify and modifyDN. If refreshes stop, the server removes the entry without notification, as if it had been deleted by an LDAP operation. A static entry cannot be turned into a dynamic one or the other way round: modifying objectClass to add dynamicObject to a static entry must return objectClassModsProhibited or objectClassViolation. A non-dynamic entry cannot be added below a dynamic entry.

Meetings can be represented as dynamic objects. The one meeting type naturally supported is the creator-owned meeting: the creating client sets the time-to-live and must refresh it. Others may join by modifying the appropriate attribute but may not refresh the entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Each dynamic entry has a countdown timer. Checking in resets the timer, and when it hits zero the entry quietly vanishes. A meeting works the same way, and only the person who made it can keep it alive.

sections.title: The Refresh Operation
sections.content:
Refresh is an LDAP ExtendedRequest whose requestName is 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.101.119.1. Its value is a DER-encoded sequence of entryName (the UTF-8 name of an existing dynamic entry) and requestTtl, a time in seconds between 1 and 31557600 that the client asks for.

The server answers with an ExtendedResponse carrying responseTtl, the lifetime it actually chose. That value must not be smaller than the one requested, and may be larger. Servers may shorten a client-requested value, but only down to a minimum of 86400 seconds (one day). Clients must be able to use the server-dictated value as their client refresh period (CRP).

On error, responseTtl is 0 and the result code says why: noSuchObject if the entry is not found, objectClassViolation if it is not dynamic, insufficientAccessRights if the requester lacks permission, and sizeLimitExceeded if requestTtl is too large. A server without the extension returns protocolError.

The request may be used when LDAP is carried over a connectionless transport. On a connection-oriented transport it need not use the same connection as any other operation. X.500/DAP servers can map it to the Modify(97) operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says, "I am still here, please keep my entry for this long." The server replies with how long it will really keep it. If the client asks for something silly, the server says no and explains why.

sections.title: Schema Additions
sections.content:
Every dynamic entry must have dynamicObject in its objectClass attribute. It is an auxiliary class (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.101.119.2) with no mandatory attributes. If the client does not supply an entryTtl value, the server provides one.

entryTtl (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.101.119.3) is an operational attribute maintained by the server that shows how many seconds the entry will continue to exist. Without refreshes, two successive reads are guaranteed to be nonincreasing, and 0 means the entry may disappear without warning. It is marked NO-USER-MODIFICATION because only the refresh operation changes it.

dynamicSubtrees (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.101.119.4) lives in the root DSE and lists the subtrees where the server supports dynamic entries, so a server can support them in only part of the directory tree.
sections.plainLanguage: A dynamic entry gets a special label saying it can expire. It also has a read-only countdown number that only a check-in can change, and the server keeps a list of which rooms have whiteboards.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
Clients find support by looking for the refresh OID in supportedExtension in the root DSE, and check dynamicSubtrees for the subtree they care about. Because Add is unchanged and does not return a lifetime, a client must send a Refresh immediately after an Add that creates a dynamic entry to learn its CRP. Clients must not refresh entries they did not create, and must be ready for a refresh to fail with noSuchObject, in which case they re-create the entry. A refresh may also fail with protocolError if a proxy without the extension takes over. A client that needs the entry gone should issue a remove request, since a timed-out entry need not vanish at once.

Servers must remove timed-out entries, though not necessarily immediately. They must enforce the structural rules, keep entryTtl present, list the OID in supportedExtension and publish the schema in the subschema subentry. Servers may require a client to bind first, for example with ACLs on entryTtl returning insufficientAccessRights (50), which can affect performance and scalability.

The RFC recommends, without requiring it, keeping dynamic entries in memory sufficient to avoid paging. If a Refresh gets no response, the client should retry immediately once, then return to its normal CRP cycle. Administrators should be able to configure a default, minimum and maximum CRP.

Replication is only partly addressed. Because entryTtl is relative, a replicated entry will be off by the replication time.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever makes an entry has to keep checking in. If a check-in gets lost, try once more right away. Servers sweep away the expired entries when they get around to it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says standard LDAP security rules apply and that the extensions add no special security issues. It notes that servers may let anonymous clients refresh entries they did not create, or may require a bind first, which has implications for performance and scalability.

It also warns that client-supplied data from a directory may be out of date. For example, an IP address in the directory may have been reassigned to another host. The RFC says this issue is not specific to LDAP or dynamic directories.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone might be allowed to keep an entry alive, so a server can ask people to show ID first. Also, an old note on the whiteboard might be wrong, so double-check before trusting it.
